title: Why is the sky blue?
examples: Teacher, does the air make the sky blue all the time?
If the atmosphere was different, would the sky still be blue?
What happens to the light when it goes through clouds?

explain.say: Sunlight actually looks like it has many colours mixed together.
These colours are all mixed together when the sun shines to us.
The air in our atmosphere scatters these colours in different ways.
Blue light scatters more easily than other colours in the air.
This scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all directions above us.
When the sun sets, the light travels through much more air.

faq.q: Why is the sky blue if sunlight has all colours?
faq.a: The sky appears blue because the air scatters the shorter blue wavelengths of light more easily than other colours. This scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all directions above us.
asks: Why does the sky look blue?
Is the blue light coming from the sky itself?

faq.q: Why are sunsets often red or orange?
faq.a: At sunrise or sunset, the sunlight has to travel through much more of the Earth's atmosphere. This long journey scatters away most of the blue light, leaving the longer red and orange colours visible. This is why the sky looks red.
asks: Does the air change the colour at sunset?

faq.q: Does this happen even if it is cloudy?
faq.a: Clouds can change how we see the sky's colour. Sometimes the clouds can block the light completely, or they can scatter the light in different ways, making the sky look grey or white.
asks: Can clouds make the sky colour change?

faq.q: Is the blue colour always the same?
faq.a: The intensity of the blue can change depending on how much atmosphere we are looking through. On very clear days, the blue scattering is very noticeable.
asks: Does the amount of air affect the blue?
Is there a limit to how blue the sky can be?

faq.q: Does the air make the colours disappear?
faq.a: No, the colours are still there in the sunlight. The air just scatters them so that we see different colours at different times of the day.
asks: Are the colours lost in the air?
Does scattering mean the colours are gone?

facts: Sunlight is composed of all the colours of the visible spectrum.
Blue light is scattered by the atmosphere more effectively than red light.
At sunrise and sunset, light travels through more atmosphere.
This long path scatters away the blue light, leaving reds and oranges visible.

quiz.say: Sunlight appears to have all of these colours:

options.show: D: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet
options.say: D: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet

quiz.why: Sunlight contains the entire visible spectrum of colours, which is why we see all of them mixed together.

wrong.1: This is tempting because the sky is blue, but sunlight contains many colours.
wrong.2: This is tempting because sunsets are red, but sunlight has all colours all the time.
wrong.3: This is tempting because some colours are visible, but sunlight is a mix of all colours.

quiz.say: What causes the sky to look blue during the day?

options.show: A: Scattering of blue light by air
options.say: A: Scattering of blue light by air

options.show: B: The sun shining blue light
options.say: B: The sun shining blue light

options.show: D: The Earth reflecting blue light
options.say: D: The Earth reflecting blue light

quiz.why: The atmosphere scatters the shorter blue wavelengths of light more easily, making the sky appear blue.

wrong.1: The sun emits all colours, not just blue light.
wrong.2: While clouds can reflect colours, the primary cause is atmospheric scattering.
wrong.3: The Earth does not generate the blue light; the atmosphere scatters the sunlight.

quiz.say: Why are sunsets often red or orange?

options.show: D: The atmosphere blocking blue light
options.say: D: The atmosphere blocking blue light

options.show: A: The air changing colour at sunset
options.say: A: The air changing colour at sunset

options.show: C: The sun only emitting red light
options.say: C: The sun only emitting red light

quiz.why: At sunset, the light travels a longer path through the atmosphere, scattering away the blues and leaving the reds and oranges visible.

wrong.0: While blue light is scattered, the effect is best described by the long path length.
wrong.2: The air itself does not change colour; the light passing through it changes appearance.
wrong.3: The sun always emits all colours, even at sunset.
